info.bio:
The Verve es una banda británica de rock y britpop, formada en Wigan, Inglaterra, en 1989. Estuvo compuesta originalmente por el vocalista Richard Ashcroft, el guitarrista Nick McCabe, el bajista Simon Jones y el baterista Peter Salisbury. Simon Tong se incorporó posteriormente como guitarrista.

Fue uno de los grupos británicos más importantes de la década de los 90, a pesar de las discusiones internas, problemas de salud, adicciones a las drogas y diversos pleitos judiciales que afectaron a sus integrantes.

scenes.name: Psicodelia británica de los noventa
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: La edad de oro de la psicodelia británica no fueron los sesenta sino los noventa: las raves crean una demanda inagotable de música inducida por (o para) las drogas. La versión pop (Telescopes, Inspiral Carpets, Verve, Sundial, Auteurs, Kula Shaker), las más sofisticadas (Curve, Cranberries, Rollerskate Skinny, Beta Band, dEUS, Gorky's Zygotic Mynci), el space-rock libre (Porcupine Tree, Terminal Cheesecake, Heads), los últimos shoegazers (Ride, Swervedriver, Spectrum y E.A.R. de Sonic Boom, Spiritualized de Jason Pierce, Flying Saucer Attack, encuentro de shoegazing y ambient) y el dream-pop (Lush, Pale Saints, Slowdive, Catherine Wheel, Bark Psychosis).

podcast.title: First Hiatus (1995-1996)
podcast.body: From September 1995 to some time in 1996, the band experienced a period that appeared to be a dissolution but was later considered a hiatus rather than a formal breakup. "There was a time from September 1995 to some time in 1996 where it looked like they were done, but they weren't."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 2

podcast.title: Guitarist's Exit Before First Breakup (1998)
podcast.body: On June 7, 1998, after a show in Rysho, Dusseldorf, Germany, singer Richard Ashcroft had a physical altercation with guitarist Nick McCabe, resulting in McCabe suffering a broken hand. McCabe subsequently decided to leave the band and was replaced by session guitarist B.J. Cole for the remaining tour commitments. "Which face took a pounding and Nick ended up with a broken hand. And with that, Nick decided he was done."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 2

podcast.title: Nick McCabe's Mental Health (1998)
podcast.body: Guitarist Nick McCabe was described as a very sensitive individual prone to emotional breakdowns, severe depression, and paranoia. His "rocky relationship with his mother" was also noted as a contributing factor. In 1998, just weeks before what was supposed to be the band's biggest tour, he announced he was quitting The Verve for good, subsequently leading a life alternating between reclusion and wandering. "Nick is a very sensitive guy and was prone to emotional breakdowns. He was prone to bouts of severe depression and paranoia and he had this really rocky relationship with his mother which somehow figured into everything."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: First Official Breakup (1999)
podcast.body: The band's proper breakup was officially announced on April 28, 1999, though they had effectively ceased to exist since their final show in Ireland on August 29, 1998, which was performed with only most of the band members. "The proper breakup of the verve came on April 28th of 1999. That's when the official announcement was made."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 2

podcast.title: Eight-Year Separation and Reunion (2007)
podcast.body: For eight years following their 1999 breakup, all members were adamant that a reunion would not happen. However, Nick McCabe began working with drummer Pete Salisbury, which prompted Richard Ashcroft to reconsider. Bass player Simon Jones was available, but guitarist Simon Tongue was deliberately excluded. The reunion was announced on June 26, 2007, after a period of eight years, one month, and 30 days apart. "For the next eight years, everyone was adamant that the verve would not reunite. The time tends to mellow people out."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 2

podcast.title: Second Breakup Over Solo Career Ambitions (2008)
podcast.body: The reunion was initially successful, especially regarding live performances, but it dissolved again around August 10, 2008. The breakup allegedly occurred because Nick McCabe and Simon Jones believed that Richard Ashcroft was using the reunion to re-establish his solo career, leading to a major conflict. "Why? Well, because Nick McCabe and Simon Jones allegedly believed that Richard Ashcroft was using this reunion just to get his solo career happening again."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 2

podcast.title: Brian Cannon Design Work
podcast.body: Brian Cannon, the art director who later designed Oasis's debut album "Definitely Maybe," had previously created artwork for The Verve. His designs for The Verve impressed Noel Gallagher, leading to their subsequent collaboration. "Noal liked what Brian had done with the verb around that time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Stories Behind Iconic Album Covers Part 2

podcast.title: Copyright Dispute and Loss of Publishing Rights
podcast.body: The Verve faced a significant legal battle over their song "Bittersweet Symphony," stemming from a licensed sample. Despite an initial agreement for 50% of earnings, Abkco Music (controlled by Allen Klein) and Andrew Loog Oldham sued, leading to The Verve being forced to surrender 100% of the song's publishing rights, resulting in Mick Jagger and Keith Richards being credited as co-writers and receiving all royalties. "Alright, give us 100% of the money made from this song or we will force you to recall every single copy of the song an album from every store and radio station and whatever worldwide."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Damage to Artistic Integrity
podcast.body: After losing control of "Bittersweet Symphony," the song was licensed by Abkco to Nike for a TV commercial in 1997. This move, perceived as the "height of selling out" at the time, severely damaged The Verve's artistic integrity in the eyes of their indie fanbase, even though the band had no control over the decision. "This destroyed the Verve's artistic integrity in the eyes of their indie fan base."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Drum Shop Owner
podcast.body: Pete Salisbury previously owned and operated a drum shop located in Stockportingwood. "I don't know if it's open anymore, but he used to run a drum shop in Stockportingwood."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: History of the Modern Drum Kit

podcast.title: Extensive Music Catalog
podcast.body: Despite "Bittersweet Symphony" being their sole Top 40 hit on the Billboard Hot 100, The Verve is widely recognized by fans for possessing a rich catalog of great songs that are deeply cherished by millions globally, indicating a legacy far beyond a single hit. "the group has a rich catalog of great songs that are near and dear to the hearts of millions of people around the world."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Great Alt-Rock One-Hit Wonders of the 90s: Part 1

podcast.title: Financial Strain and Legal History
podcast.body: The band faced significant financial hardship and lacked the resources to continue extensive legal battles over "Bitter Sweet Symphony." They had previously experienced very negative outcomes with legal processes, which likely influenced their decision to agree to unfavorable settlements to avoid further, potentially endless, and costly litigation. "estos procesos legales se te antojaban carísimos e interminables y el grupo de ver tampoco tenía este si vos recursos para afrontar nuevas legales ya había tenido muy malas experiencias con nuevas legales anteriormente."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Bitter Sweet Symphony: Quien fue su verdadero compositor?

podcast.title: Frequent Breakups and Reformations
podcast.body: The Verve was characterized as a "flaky" band, frequently breaking up and reforming throughout their career. These instabilities were attributed to underlying reasons, primarily involving guitarist Nick McCabe and, to a lesser extent, singer Richard Ashcroft. "they were a little flaky breaking up and reforming all the time but there were some underlying reasons behind all that."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Grammy Credit Discrepancy
podcast.body: "Bittersweet Symphony" was nominated for a Grammy Award for Best Song, but the ballot controversially listed the songwriters as "Jagger Richards," reflecting the outcome of the publishing dispute rather than Richard Ashcroft's original composition. "And the ballot listed the songwriters of Bitter Sweet Symphony as Jagger Richards."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence on Sigur Rós
podcast.body: The Verve is cited as an important influence for Sigur Rós, alongside dream pop acts like the Cocteau Twins and Radiohead's later work. "Dreampop, the Cocktoe twins are very important here, along with the Verve and anything Radiohead did with OK Computer and Beyond."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What Exactly is Post Rock? Part 2

podcast.title: Loss of Song Rights
podcast.body: The Verve faced immense legal pressure and high costs due to lawsuits initiated by Allen Klein regarding "Bitter Sweet Symphony." Despite having initially secured permission for the sampled portion, the escalating legal battles and their financial strain led The Verve to agree to an extrajudicial settlement, resulting in Allen Klein acquiring 100% of the song's rights. This agreement, while surrendering all control, allowed them to avoid potentially ruinous indemnification costs. "perderían todo derecho y control sobre la canción pero al menos no tenía que indemnizarlo y no tenía que pasar años gastando injecentes candidades de dinero en la bogados."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Bitter Sweet Symphony: Quien fue su verdadero compositor?

podcast.title: Manchester Origin
podcast.body: The Verve is included in a list of numerous artists with roots in Manchester. "Verve."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Manchester Origins
podcast.body: The Verve are listed among the numerous bands from Manchester, emphasizing the city's prolific musical output. "loads of loads of Aces, Buzcocs of Fall, James, Godly and Cream, Badly Drone Boy, Elbow, you know, John Mayl, Star Sailor-Verb, Phil Linnett, group of Manchester, Smith and you are a simply red, all his, you know, he goes on and on and this, this is bands and bands and bands, you know."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Oral History of Manchester Part 2

podcast.title: Multiple 21st Century Reunions
podcast.body: The Verve was noted for having reunited "again" in the first decade of the 21st century, highlighting their participation in the trend of alt-rock bands reforming to boost the scene's temporary vitality and re-engage former fans. "In addition, the Pixies...the Verve again...These reunions injected some life into the scene, albeit temporary life."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Oasis Touring with The Verve
podcast.body: Much of the songwriting for Oasis's "Don't Look Back In Anger" came together over just two days, primarily during sound checks while Oasis was on tour with The Verve. "much of it came together in just two days while touring with the verb Sound checks mostly"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Out-of-the-Box Rhythms
podcast.body: Pete Salisbury is noted for his unique and unconventional drumming rhythms, which significantly contributed to The Verve's sound, moving beyond simple 4/4 beats. His playing often involves complex interplay between his left hand on the snare and his right foot on the bass drum. "No simple 4 or 4 beats from him."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: History of the Modern Drum Kit

podcast.title: Permission for Instrumental Sample
podcast.body: The Verve had originally requested and received permission from Andrew Loog Oldham to use his instrumental verse, specifically "5 notas de manera repetitiva," as a base for their song "Bitter Sweet Symphony." They then developed a completely new song around this element. This initial agreement was later overshadowed by further legal disputes as the song gained immense popularity and profitability. "ellos originalmente ya habían pedido por miso a Adam Coleman para usar su verso instrumental y él es aviado el visto bueno, había solicitado a 5 notas de manera repetitiva de como base de la canción y realmente ellos hicieron una canción completamente nueva."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Bitter Sweet Symphony: Quien fue su verdadero compositor?

podcast.title: Post-Britpop Heroes
podcast.body: The Verve emerged as new heroes for music fans after the decline of Britpop, indicating a shift in musical taste among the audience who had grown up and moved on from the Britpop era. "Their new heroes were Radiohead and the Verve and eventually Coldplay."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock: Chapter 12

podcast.title: Reunion for Touring
podcast.body: The Verve were one of many bands from past decades that reunited in the 21st century, a trend largely motivated by financial incentives. With declining CD sales impacting artist revenues, returning to the touring circuit offered a lucrative way to appeal to nostalgic fan bases and fill large venues. "The list of reunions is long."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 1: (100-91)

podcast.title: Reunions for Solo Career Launch
podcast.body: Richard Ashcroft was criticized for orchestrating some reunions of The Verve primarily to boost his solo career, using the band to regain prominence before leaving them again. "esto es algo que por ejemplo se da chaco muchísimo a richadas que ofren algunas aroniones de los de ver que la había hecho un poco para intentar lanzar su carrera en solitario entonces volvía a conocer ver volvía a estar peda candelero y los volvía a dejar en la cuneita."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Vuelven los Smashing Pumpkins... mas o menos

podcast.title: Richard Ashcroft's Car Incident
podcast.body: Richard Ashcroft once engaged in an act of vandalism by doing "donuts" with his car on someone's lawn until all the wheels came off the vehicle. "Then there was a time he did donuts with his car and someone's lawn until all the wheels came off."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Richard Ashcroft's Disappearance
podcast.body: At one point, singer Richard Ashcroft disappeared for five days, with no one knowing his whereabouts during that time. "Once he just disappeared for five days, nobody knew where he was."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Richard Ashcroft's Eviction and Debt
podcast.body: After finishing a tour, Richard Ashcroft returned home to discover that his landlord had changed the locks to his apartment and sold off all his possessions, including his record collection. This was due to Richard owing three thousand pounds in back rents. With only a single plastic bag containing his remaining belongings, he moved to London to "sponge off friends," without even a change of clothing. "Richard came home to find that his landlord had changed the locks to Richard's apartment and had sold off anything that was inside including his record collection because Richard owed three thousand pounds in back rents."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Rise of New Alternative Bands (Mid-90s)
podcast.body: The Verve was one of the new bands emerging in the mid-1990s as alternative music gained widespread acceptance. "We had new bands like Weezer and Rage Against the Machine and Beck and the Cranberries in the Verve."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

concerts.title: Paris Show (April 18, 1995)
concerts.body: Oasis opened a show for The Verve in Paris on April 18, 1995. It was on this rainy night, after returning from a strip club, that Noel Gallagher wrote "Don't Look Back In Anger." "Noll wrote it in a day, or more specifically, on a rainy night in Paris, as Oasis was opening a show for the Verve."

xref.title: Catalog Ownership Pre-1970
xref.body: Material released by The Rolling Stones before 1970 was owned by Abko Records, run by Allan Klein. This complicated the sampling clearance for The Verve's "Bittersweet Symphony," as Decca Records, which held the copyright to The Rolling Stones Songbook, did not control all the necessary rights. "Material release before 1970 was owned by Abco Records, run by Alan Klein, who had succeeded Andrew Geoldem as the Stones manager."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Album Artwork Collaboration (1993-1998)
xref.body: Noel Gallagher first met designer Brian Cannon about a year before Oasis's debut album and was impressed by his work for The Verve, bonding over Adidas running shoe designs. Noel specifically requested Cannon to design Oasis's artwork once they were signed, a collaboration that continued for the next four years, covering their early albums and singles. "Telling Brian, when we get signed, I want you to do our artwork."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Roskilde Cancellation (2000)
xref.body: The Wases (The Verve) cancelled their set at the Roskilde Festival on June 30, 2000, due to concerns that the organizers did not have adequate safety measures or their "act together" amidst heavy rain and muddy conditions. "Both the Wases and the Pet Shop boys had canceled their sets because they didn't think organizers had their act together."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Roskilde Festival Tragedy (2000)
xref.body: On June 30, 2000, Pearl Jam performed at the Roskilde Festival in Denmark during its second day, following heavy rains that left 100,000 attendees soaked and safety concerns that led other bands like The Verve and Pet Shop Boys to cancel. During Pearl Jam's 11:30 PM set, a crowd surge pushed attendees against a steel barrier down a slight, muddy incline. Vocalist Eddie Vedder repeatedly stopped the band, imploring the crowd to move back as the crush became a "slow-motion avalanche of bodies." Ultimately, 26 people were injured, and 8 bodies were pulled from the pile, with another person dying later in hospital. The victims were from Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, and Sweden. "Our lives will never be the same, but we know that this is nothing compared to the grief of the families and friends of those involved."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: "Bittersweet Symphony" Remix (mid-90s)
xref.body: Dreadbase is a DJ/producer whose remix of The Verve's "Bittersweet Symphony" in the mid-90s was a life-changing song for Ash. This particular remix profoundly inspired Ash's vision for USS, motivating him to integrate melody and simplicity into electronic music, aiming to "bring melody to the robot" and "bring a heart to the robot." "He did this remix of Bittersweet Symphony in the mid 90s and I heard that and I said that's what we're that's what I need to do."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: USS In Their Own Words: Part 1

xref.title: 21st Century Reunion
xref.body: The Pixies were listed as one of the significant alt-rock acts that reunited in the first decade of the 21st century, contributing to a temporary resurgence of interest and energy in the scene. "In addition, the Pixies, smashing pumpkins, the lemon heads, rage against the machine, my bloody Valentine, blink 182, garbage, Jesus and Marychain, the Verve again."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Arranger of "The Last Time" String Figure
xref.body: David Whitaker was the orchestrator hired to arrange the string figure in the 1966 Andrew Loog Oldham Orchestra's version of The Rolling Stones' "The Last Time." This six-second string figure, which he composed and arranged, became central to The Verve's "Bittersweet Symphony" lawsuit. Despite his pivotal role in creating the sampled material, he received no additional compensation beyond his initial fee in 1966. "They were written and arranged by an orchestrator for higher guy named David Whitaker."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Credited on "Bittersweet Symphony"
xref.body: After Allan Klein gained control of The Verve's "Bittersweet Symphony" rights, he controversially added Mick Jagger and Keith Richards' names to all songwriting credits on the song and The Verve's album Urban Hymns, despite them not composing the sampled string figure. "who then slapped the names Jagger Richards on all the copies of the song and the album Urban Hymns."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Credited on "Bittersweet Symphony"
xref.body: Following Allan Klein's acquisition of the rights to The Verve's "Bittersweet Symphony," he assigned songwriting credits to Keith Richards and Mick Jagger on all copies of the song and the album Urban Hymns, even though neither composed the sampled musical phrase. "who then slapped the names Jagger Richards on all the copies of the song and the album Urban Hymns."

xref.body: Noel Gallagher wrote "Don't Look Back In Anger" on a rainy night in Paris, specifically after returning from a strip club, on April 18, 1995, while Oasis was opening for The Verve. "or even more specifically, after Noll had come back from a strip club."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.body: The Cocteau Twins are cited as very important in the dream pop influences for Sigur Rós. "Dreampop, the Cocktoe twins are very important here, along with the Verve and anything Radiohead did with OK Computer and Beyond."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influences
xref.body: Sigur Rós draws from shoegaze traditions, citing My Bloody Valentine and Ride, as well as dream pop influences like the Cocteau Twins, The Verve, and Radiohead's work from *OK Computer* and beyond. "Siger-Rus, which means victory rose, by the way, comes from the tradition of groups into Shugays, such as My Bloody Valentine and Ride."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What Exactly is Post Rock? Part 2

xref.title: Influential Sound
xref.body: My Bloody Valentine, an Irish band, pushed guitar noise and "walls of sound" to new levels, subsequently influencing a vast number of bands. Their sonic approach impacted groups such as The Verve, The Smashing Pumpkins, Nine Inch Nails, Silver Sun Pickups, Garbage, and Nirvana, as well as an uncountable number of shoegaze and fuzz bands. "My Bloody Valentine, an Irish band that took guitar noise and walls of sound to new levels, influencing scores of new bands..."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 2

xref.title: Lawsuit for Royalties
xref.body: Andrew Loog Oldham, who was the original manager of The Rolling Stones, sued The Verve, claiming they owed him $1.7 million in royalties for "Bittersweet Symphony" due to the use of a five-note progression from his orchestra's version of "The Last Time." "Lugoldem figured he was owed $1.7 million."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Originator of "Bittersweet Symphony" Snippet
xref.body: David Whitaker was the orchestral arranger who originally wrote the distinctive five-note progression in Andrew Loog Oldham's version of "The Last Time." This specific musical phrase later served as the inspiration and sampled basis for The Verve's "Bittersweet Symphony." "He wrote that five note bit."

He was later succeeded by Allan Klein. "Andrew Lou Geoldem, the manager of the Rolling Stones back in the day."
